title: How Buffett judged managers by return on equity, and bought stocks like whole businesses (1977 letter)
summary: Buffett argues record EPS means little when equity compounds, so return on equity is the real measure. He explains buying marketable stocks as if buying whole businesses, why insurance magnifies manager quality, and why tailwind businesses beat headwind ones like textiles.

principles.text: Judge managers by return on equity capital, not record earnings per share, since retained equity compounds EPS automatically.
principles.quote: we believe a more appropriate measure of managerial economic performance to be return on equity capital.

principles.text: Buy stocks with the same four tests used to buy whole businesses: understandable, good prospects, honest management, attractive price.
principles.quote: We want the business to be (1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price.

principles.text: Welcome lower prices on stocks you own when the business still satisfies you; do not trade for short-term price moves.
principles.quote: In fact, if their business experience continues to satisfy us, we welcome lower market prices of stocks we own as an opportunity to acquire even more of a good thing at a better price.

principles.text: Minority stakes in outstanding businesses can be bargains unavailable through whole-company acquisition.
principles.quote: Our experience has been that pro-rata portions of truly outstanding businesses sometimes sell in the securities markets at very large discounts from the prices they would command in negotiated transactions involving entire companies.

principles.text: Prefer businesses with tailwinds over headwinds; good management cannot rescue a structurally poor industry.
principles.quote: One of the lessons your management has learned - and, unfortunately, sometimes re-learned - is the importance of being in businesses where tailwinds prevail rather than headwinds.

principles.text: In insurance, discipline means giving up volume when rates turn inadequate, even though institutions resist letting rivals take business.
principles.quote: Unusual managerial discipline will be required, as it runs counter to normal institutional behavior to let the other fellow take away business - even at foolish prices.
